Path: get_or_create_elevenlabs_client(current_user.id, session) (line 1354, and 535) calls ElevenLabsClientManager.get_client, whose whole lookup is guarded by `if cls._instance is None:` (line 177), so variable_service.get_variable(user_id=user_id, name="ELEVENLABS_API_KEY", ...) is executed only for the very first caller; cls._api_key and cls._instance are class attributes that live for the lifetime of the process and are never keyed or reset, so every later caller receives the client built with the first user's ElevenLabs API key. Nothing checks that the cached key belongs to current_user.id, and no code path clears _api_key/_instance on logout, key rotation or user deletion. Impact: line 1358 (elevenlabs_client.voices.get_all()) returns the other user's voice library, including their private/cloned voices, to whoever calls the endpoint next, and audio generation at lines 905-912 and 1288-1295 is executed against the first user's ElevenLabs account and credits. Fix: cache clients per user (dict keyed by user id) or resolve the caller's own ELEVENLABS_API_KEY on every request, never falling back to another user's cached secret, and invalidate the cached client when a user's key changes.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS with credentials lets any site read refresh tokens and take over accounts
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/login.py:123 (POST /api/v1/refresh), reached from any web page the victim visits; the attacker's input is the browser's Origin header on a cross-site request, which main.py:294-300 answers.
Attacker: any website the victim visits, crossing into the victim's authenticated Langflow session by reading the body of a credentialed cross-origin request.
Path: create_app adds CORSMiddleware with the hardcoded origins = ["*"] and allow_credentials=True (main.py:292-300). The victim is logged in, so the browser holds refresh_token_lf, which is set with SameSite=None by default (services/settings/auth.py:40 REFRESH_SAME_SITE = "none", applied at login.py:42-50). The attacker's page runs fetch("https://victim/api/v1/refresh", {method:"POST", credentials:"include"}); Starlette's CORSMiddleware, with allow_credentials=True, reflects the requesting Origin (with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true) instead of "*" for preflights and for requests that carry a Cookie header, so both the preflight and the response are allowed for any origin. login.py:131-153 reads the refresh cookie, mints new tokens and returns them in the JSON body, which the attacker's origin can now read. Nothing stops it: create_app registers only ContentSizeLimitMiddleware, CORSMiddleware and JavaScriptMIMETypeMiddleware, so there is no CSRF token, no Origin/Referer check and no allow-list anywhere on this route; allow_origins is not read from configuration at all.
Impact: full account takeover. The attacker obtains a valid access token and can call every API endpoint as the victim (list/read flows and their embedded configuration, read stored variables/secrets, create custom components); even if a browser refused to expose the body, the credentialed POST still executes, so the endpoint is also unprotected CSRF.
Fix: replace origins = ["*"] with the explicit list of Langflow's own origins (loaded from settings), never combine a wildcard origin with allow_credentials=True, and add CSRF protection to the cookie-authenticated endpoints such as /api/v1/refresh.

findings.title: JWT cookies lack HttpOnly/Secure and allow cross-site use, enabling token theft
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/login.py:51 (access_token_lf cookie) and login.py:42/135 (refresh_token_lf cookie), using the defaults defined at services/settings/auth.py:40-51.
Attacker: any script that runs in the application's origin (for example injected through rendered flow output or a custom component) or a passive network attacker on plain HTTP, crossing into the victim's session credential.
Path: REFRESH_SAME_SITE defaults to "none" (line 40), ACCESS_SECURE to False (line 48) and ACCESS_HTTPONLY to False (line 50). login.py:51-59 stores the JWT access token in the access_token_lf cookie with httponly=False and secure=False, login.py:42-50 stores the refresh token with SameSite=None, and login.py:135-152 repeats the same flags on every refresh. That same access_token_lf cookie is accepted as the WebSocket credential by services/auth/utils.py:225, so the token is the single bearer secret for the whole API.
Impact: the access token is readable from JavaScript (document.cookie) and therefore stealable by any XSS, and it is transmitted in cleartext over HTTP because Secure is off; SameSite=None on the refresh cookie means /api/v1/refresh accepts cross-site requests, which together with the permissive CORS configuration is what turns a visited web page into session theft.
Fix: ship ACCESS_HTTPONLY=True and ACCESS_SECURE=True, keep REFRESH_HTTPONLY/REFRESH_SECURE true and set REFRESH_SAME_SITE to "lax" or "strict" (or keep a same-site refresh endpoint plus a CSRF token) so the cookies cannot be read by scripts or attached to cross-site requests.

findings.title: Unauthenticated WebSocket callers grow voice_config_cache without bound
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/voice_mode.py:734 (WebSocket route /ws/flow_as_tool/{flow_id}/{session_id} defined at line 719; the no-session route at line 702 reaches the same call with a fresh uuid4 key).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the authentication boundary, because the cache is written before get_current_user_for_websocket is called on line 735.
Path: the attacker-chosen session_id path parameter is passed to get_voice_config at line 734; get_voice_config (lines 203-209) executes voice_config_cache[session_id] = VoiceConfig(session_id) for any unseen key, storing it in the module-global dict declared at line 513.
Nothing on the path stops it: the route declares no dependencies and the router is mounted without auth (api/router.py:49), the credential check happens only after the insert, and no code ever evicts the cache - there is no max size, no TTL, no LRU, and the cleanup in the finally block (lines 1113-1127) only closes sockets and tasks. Reconnecting with a new session_id, or simply using the no-session route whose key is a fresh uuid4 each time, leaves another entry behind after the connection is gone.
Impact: every unauthenticated connection permanently retains a VoiceConfig object in the API worker, so memory grows without bound until the worker is OOM-killed or restarted, denying service to every user of that worker; attacker-chosen keys additionally let unrelated sessions collide on the same cached object.
Fix: create and cache the VoiceConfig only after successful authentication (move the get_voice_config call below the auth check), key the cache by authenticated user and session, cap it with an LRU/TTL or max-entries policy, and delete the entry when the WebSocket closes.

findings.title: Unauthenticated RCE via exec() in code validation endpoint
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/validate.py:13-16 (POST /api/v1/validate/code -> validate_code(code.code)).
Attacker: an unauthenticated HTTP caller, crossing the login boundary into arbitrary server-side code execution (with the shipped defaults AUTO_LOGIN=True and skip_auth_auto_login=True, services/auth/utils.py:51-66 returns the superuser for a request with no token and no API key, so the CurrentActiveUser dependency passes anonymously; with auto-login disabled, any authenticated user reaches it).
Path: the request body field code is passed unchanged to validate_code (utils/validate.py:24), which ast.parses it and, for every ast.FunctionDef, compiles the node and calls exec(code_obj) at line 57; the import loop above only calls importlib.import_module and never restricts the AST.
Nothing on the path stops it: there is no sandbox, no node-type allow-list and no literal-only check, and exec of a FunctionDef evaluates its decorator expressions and default-argument expressions at definition time, so a body such as '@evil()\ndef f(): pass' or 'def f(x=evil()): pass' runs code before any validation result is returned; the try/except only records the exception after execution.
Impact for this application: the payload runs in the Langflow server process with the process's filesystem, environment (API keys, SECRET_KEY, DB credentials) and network reach, i.e. full remote code execution and access to every user's flows and variables.
Fix: do not exec during validation; walk the AST and validate node types and constant defaults only, reject non-literal decorators and default values, or run the check in a disposable sandbox with no secrets and no network, and require real authentication (AUTO_LOGIN=false / LANGFLOW_SKIP_AUTH_AUTO_LOGIN=false) for this route.

findings.title: Unauthenticated RCE via exec of custom component code
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/endpoints.py:652-659 (POST /api/v1/custom_component, body raw_code.code; the same path is used by /api/v1/custom_component/update at endpoints.py:674-698 and by flow build/run).
Attacker: any caller who can reach the API - unauthenticated under the shipped auto-login defaults described above, otherwise any authenticated user - crossing from 'build me a component template' into execution of the submitted program inside the server process.
Path: raw_code.code -> Component(_code=...) -> build_custom_component_template (custom/utils.py:443) -> run_build_config (custom/utils.py:344) -> eval_custom_component_code (custom/eval.py:12) -> create_class (utils/validate.py:172) -> prepare_global_scope (utils/validate.py:232), which compiles every module-level ClassDef/FunctionDef/Assign and calls exec(compiled_code, exec_globals) at line 293.
Nothing on the path stops it: the code is only ast.parsed to separate imports from definitions, the imports are loaded with importlib, and then the definitions themselves are compiled and executed in the server process with no sandbox, no allow-list and no privilege check beyond the (default-bypassed) login; the _user_id passed down is just an attribute.
Impact for this application: arbitrary Python executes as the Langflow server (module-level expressions, class bodies and decorators), giving full filesystem, environment and network access and control of the backend.
Fix: parse user code for metadata only and never exec it in the API process; if the code must run, run it in an isolated worker/container with no secrets, no DB and no network, and gate component execution on a real authenticated identity.

findings.title: Unauthenticated CPU exhaustion via quadratic prompt validation
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/validate.py:26-41 (POST /api/v1/validate/prompt) - this route has no authentication dependency at all, so it is reachable anonymously regardless of settings. Attacker: an unauthenticated caller crossing into server-wide CPU starvation. The `template` field flows into process_prompt_template -> validate_prompt -> _check_input_variables -> _fix_variable, whose loop performs `if var not in wrong_variables` - a linear scan of a list that grows with every attacker-supplied variable - and _check_variable (line 83) scans the shared, growing invalid_chars list with `char in invalid_chars`, while _check_for_errors (line 91) does `var not in fixed_variables` over another list inside a loop. All three are O(N) inside a loop over N caller-controlled variables, making the endpoint quadratic: a template of the form `{a0.b}{a1.b}...` (each name is invalid because of the dot) with roughly 150k variables in a 1 MB body forces on the order of 10^10 string comparisons before an error is returned, and the default 100 MB body cap (settings.max_file_size_upload=100) leaves room for millions of variables. Impact: a single unauthenticated request keeps a CPU core busy for minutes to hours, and repeated requests starve all other users. Fix: use sets for wrong_variables, invalid_chars and fixed_variables (or reject templates over a small length and cap the variable count) so validation stays linear.

findings.title: Unauthenticated download of any flow's uploaded files (no auth or owner check)
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:74 (@router.get("/download/{flow_id}/{file_name}"))
Attacker: any unauthenticated network caller (and any logged-in user against another user's flows), crossing the authentication and per-user ownership boundary for files uploaded to flows.
The handler download_file declares only file_name, flow_id and storage_service. Unlike its siblings upload_file (line 44), list_files (line 171) and delete_file (line 185), it has no CurrentActiveUser dependency and no Annotated[Flow, Depends(get_flow)] ownership check. file_name and flow_id go directly into storage_service.get_file(flow_id=flow_id_str, file_name=file_name) at line 92, which LocalStorageService resolves as self.data_dir / flow_id / file_name (src/backend/base/langflow/services/storage/local.py:58) and returns the raw bytes. Nothing verifies the flow exists or that it belongs to the caller, and no guard exists at the app level either: api/router.py:43 includes files_router without dependencies and create_app (src/backend/base/langflow/main.py:275-346) installs no authentication middleware, only CORS/size checks; the generated spec shows no security requirement for this operation (docs/openapi.json:3334). Impact: anyone who knows a flow UUID and a file name (flow links are shared, IDs appear in logs/chat sessions) can download every document or file users uploaded to that flow without logging in; any authenticated user can do the same for other users' flows, defeating the owner check get_flow enforces on every sibling route. file_name is also unsanitized before the path join, so on Windows '..\' sequences escape the flow directory. Fix: add the flow: Annotated[Flow, Depends(get_flow)] dependency (which also enforces flow.user_id == current_user.id), and reject file names containing '/', '\' or '..' or verify Path(data_dir/flow_id/file_name).resolve().is_relative_to(data_dir).

findings.title: Authenticated user can write arbitrary files via unsanitized upload filename
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v2/files.py:81 (@router.post("") upload_user_file, which calls save_file_routine at line 110)
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the boundary of their own per-user storage folder and reaching arbitrary paths on the server filesystem.
The multipart filename is fully client-controlled: save_file_routine sets file_name = file.filename (line 73) and passes it unsanitized to storage_service.save_file(flow_id=str(current_user.id), file_name=file_name, data=file_content) (line 76). LocalStorageService.save_file (src/backend/base/langflow/services/storage/local.py:33-38) builds folder_path = self.data_dir / flow_id and file_path = folder_path / file_name and opens file_path for writing, so a filename such as '../../../../tmp/evil' (or '../../langflow.db') resolves outside config_dir/<user id>/; the same unsanitized string is persisted in UserFile.path (line 158). Nothing on the path strips path separators: the only upload-specific middleware (src/backend/base/langflow/main.py:303-336) validates the multipart boundary and body framing, not the filename, and no other validation exists in the endpoint or the storage service. Impact: an ordinary user gets arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content and name anywhere the Langflow process can write (overwriting the SQLite database, .env/config, plugin or startup files), which is a full escape of the per-user file sandbox and can lead to data destruction or code execution. Fix: store the file under a generated UUID or Path(file.filename).name only, reject names containing '/', '\' or '..', and assert the resolved path stays inside data_dir/<user_id> before writing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated arbitrary file read via profile picture path traversal
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:128 (@router.get("/profile_pictures/{folder_name}/{file_name}"))
Attacker: any unauthenticated network caller, crossing the authentication boundary and (on Windows) the config-directory boundary.
The handler takes folder_name and file_name from the path, builds folder_path = config_path / "profile_pictures" / folder_name (line 138) and calls storage_service.get_file(flow_id=folder_path, file_name=file_name) at line 140, which LocalStorageService resolves as self.data_dir / flow_id / file_name; because folder_path is an absolute Path, the data_dir prefix is discarded and the read targets config_dir/profile_pictures/<folder_name>/<file_name>. There is no CurrentActiveUser dependency and no authorization check, and no app-level middleware requires a login (api/router.py:43, src/backend/base/langflow/main.py:275-346). folder_name is not validated, so on Windows an absolute value such as 'C:\Windows' (sent URL-encoded as C%3A%5CWindows) makes the path join escape config_dir entirely and turns this into unauthenticated arbitrary file read; on other platforms it still exposes every file under config_dir/profile_pictures without authentication. Fix: require an authenticated user on this route (and on /profile_pictures/list), whitelist folder_name to known values such as 'People'/'Space', and verify the resolved path is inside config_dir/profile_pictures.

findings.title: Stored XSS via inline-served SVG in /files/images download endpoint
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:103
Attacker: any user who can upload a file to a flow (with the default auto-login configuration, any caller), crossing into a victim's browser session on the Langflow origin via stored XSS.
The route derives the media type from the file extension; "svg" maps to image/svg+xml in services/storage/constants.py:11, which passes the startswith("image") check at line 118, and the response at line 123 sets no Content-Disposition. A user uploads an SVG containing a <script> to their own flow through /files/upload (the upload route stores any extension), then sends the victim the URL /api/v1/files/images/<flow_id>/<timestamp>_x.svg. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated and returns the stored bytes inline as an SVG document, the script executes in the application's origin when the victim opens the link, allowing theft of session tokens and API calls as the victim. Fix: force Content-Disposition: attachment and a restrictive Content-Security-Policy (or serve user files from a separate origin), and exclude image/svg+xml from the inline-serving allow-list.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can OOM worker by buffering whole upload body in middleware
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:40 (POST /api/v1/files/upload/{flow_id}).
Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller, crossing the server's configured upload-size limit (max_file_size_upload, default 100 MB in services/settings/base.py:219) and its memory boundary; no credentials or valid flow id are needed because the middleware runs before routing and before the get_flow/CurrentActiveUser dependencies.
Path: create_app() adds ContentSizeLimitMiddleware at main.py:287 and then registers check_boundary with @app.middleware("http") at main.py:303. Starlette's add_middleware inserts each new middleware at the front of user_middleware and build_middleware_stack wraps that list in reverse, so check_boundary executes outside (before) ContentSizeLimitMiddleware. For any request whose path contains "/api/v1/files/upload" (main.py:305), check_boundary executes `body = await request.body()` at main.py:322, which drains the ASGI receive channel and concatenates every chunk into a single in-memory bytes object. ContentSizeLimitMiddleware's receive_wrapper (middleware.py:29-51), which is supposed to abort once max_file_size_upload MB have been received, never sees the raw stream; and the route's own guard `if file.size > max_file_size_upload * 1024 * 1024` (api/v1/files.py:54) can only run after FastAPI's multipart parser has consumed the whole body, i.e., after the buffering has already happened.
Why nothing on the path stops it: the only size guard is ordered behind the unbounded read; the boundary regex at main.py:316 is applied to the header only and the body is read regardless of its size; no authentication dependency runs before middleware.
Impact: a single unauthenticated POST (Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=x is enough to enter the branch) with a multi-gigabyte body makes a worker allocate that much RAM before any rejection, and repeated or concurrent requests OOM-kill the service; even accepted uploads lose Starlette's normal disk-spooling behavior (file parts spool after 1 MB) and are held entirely in memory.
Fix: do not read the request body in check_boundary; validate only the Content-Type/boundary headers or stream-validate with a hard byte cap. Register ContentSizeLimitMiddleware as the outermost middleware (add it after the @app.middleware definitions) so the limit is enforced while the body streams, or read the body with a bounded reader that raises after max_file_size_upload bytes.

findings.title: Tiny upload with LIKE wildcard forces full-table scan of all users' files
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v2/files.py:81-82 (POST /api/v2/files and /api/v2/files/), the filename of the uploaded multipart part.
Attacker: any authenticated user the deployment issues an account to, crossing the per-user data boundary: the query has no user filter, so it scans and materializes every user's file rows, and its cost is set by the size of the whole global file table rather than by the attacker's request.
Path: `new_filename = file.filename` (line 117) is split at the last dot (lines 119-121) into root_filename, which is then interpolated unescaped and unfiltered into `select(UserFile).where(col(UserFile.name).like(f"{root_filename}%"))` (line 131); `existing_files.all()` (line 133) materializes every matching row into memory, and each row's name is run through `re.search(r"\((\d+)\)(?=\.\w+$|$)", ...)` (lines 139-142). Because `%` and `_` are SQL LIKE wildcards and no ESCAPE clause is used, an upload named `%.txt` yields the pattern `%%`, matching every row of the file table for all users; even an ordinary prefix such as `a` matches all users' files starting with that prefix. Nothing between the entry point and the query escapes the wildcards or adds `UserFile.user_id == current_user.id`, and the uploaded file itself can be a few bytes, so the request is small and cheap.
Why nothing on the path stops it: the only related check, `get_file_by_name` (lines 172-185), is used on a different branch (the _mcp_servers special case) and does filter by user, but the normal-file branch at lines 130-145 never applies that filter or escaping.
Impact: each tiny upload forces a full table scan plus in-memory materialization of the entire global file table and a regex pass over it, i.e., O(total files in the deployment) work and memory for an O(1) request, repeatable to exhaust the worker; it also lets one tenant's uploads affect the rename count computed for another tenant's records.
Fix: constrain the query to the current user (`where(UserFile.user_id == current_user.id)`) and escape LIKE metacharacters in root_filename before building the pattern (escape `\`, `%`, `_` and use `like(pattern, escape="\\")`), and compute the maximum count in SQL instead of loading all matching rows into memory.

findings.title: Unauthenticated POST /validate/prompt runs server prompt validation and leaks errors
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/validate.py:26 (POST /api/v1/validate/prompt). Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the login boundary that the rest of the API (and the sibling /validate/code endpoint at line 14, which requires CurrentActiveUser) enforces. Path: anonymous POST body -> post_validate_prompt (line 27, no auth dependency on the signature) -> process_prompt_template -> validate_prompt -> extract_input_variables_from_prompt and PromptTemplate construction, with any exception echoed to the caller as HTTP 500 detail=str(e) at line 48. Nothing on the path authenticates or authorizes the caller; the router is mounted without a global auth dependency (api/router.py:36, main.py:370), so the missing dependency on this handler is the only check and it is absent. Impact: outsiders can drive the server's prompt-processing/validation code with no credentials (unauthenticated resource use and an oracle for the validation logic), while every other /api/v1 endpoint requires an active user; any internal exception text from prompt processing is also returned to them. Fix: add '_current_user: CurrentActiveUser' to the handler signature (as /validate/code does) and return a generic error message instead of str(e).

findings.title: Authenticated user can build/execute vertices of any other user's flow
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:256 (POST /build/{flow_id}/vertices/{vertex_id}).
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing into another user's flow execution.
Path: flow_id (path), vertex_id (path) and the `inputs` body are taken from the request; the handler reads the graph from the chat-service cache with `chat_service.get_cache(flow_id_str)` (chat.py:292/297) and, on a cache miss, loads it straight from the database with build_graph_from_db(flow_id=flow_id, ...) (chat.py:301-305), which ends in `session.get(Flow, flow_id)` (api/utils.py:187) with no ownership test; it then calls `graph.build_vertex(vertex_id=..., user_id=str(current_user.id), inputs_dict=inputs.model_dump() if inputs else {}, files=files, ...)` (chat.py:313-320) and returns the built component's result and artifacts in VertexBuildResponse.
Nothing stops it: the only dependency is `current_user: CurrentActiveUser` (chat.py:264), i.e. authentication, and no branch in build_vertex, build_graph_from_db, build_graph_from_db_no_cache or Graph.build_vertex (graph/graph/base.py:1390-1464, which forwards inputs_dict straight to `vertex.build(inputs=...)`) checks that the flow belongs to the caller. The cache used as the primary source (ChatService.set_cache/get_cache, services/chat/service.py:21-56) is keyed by the flow id string alone, so graphs produced by other users are reused for whoever names the same flow_id.
Impact: a user can execute arbitrary vertices of any other user's flow with attacker-chosen input values and read the resulting outputs, and can drive side effects in that flow (messages persisted under the victim's flow, outbound calls), while bypassing the ownership filtering that /run and the flows API apply.
Fix: verify ownership of flow_id (join Flow and compare user_id with current_user.id, allowing the AUTO_LOGIN/None-owner case) before consulting the cache or building the graph, and scope the chat-service cache key by the owning user as defense in depth.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller can poison any flow's build cache and hijack its execution
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:71 (POST /build/{flow_id}/vertices, deprecated).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing into any user's flow and into a shared cache that other users' builds read from.
Path: the handler takes only `flow_id` (path) and an optional `data` body plus `session: DbSession` (chat.py:79) - there is no CurrentActiveUser dependency at all, unlike its sibling build_flow (chat.py:153) and build_vertex (chat.py:264). With no `data`, it calls build_graph_from_db(flow_id=flow_id, session=session, chat_service=chat_service) (chat.py:104), which loads any flow by id from the database (api/utils.py:195 -> 187) and then caches it under the raw flow id; with `data`, it calls build_and_cache_graph_from_data(flow_id=flow_id, graph_data=data.model_dump(), chat_service=chat_service) (chat.py:106-108), which builds a Graph from the caller's JSON and stores it at `chat_service.set_cache(str_flow_id, graph)` (api/utils.py:209-210).
Nothing stops it: no authentication dependency, no ownership lookup, and the cache key is just `str(flow_id)`; the response returns the graph's first-layer and runnable vertex ids (chat.py:125). The same flow-id-keyed cache is the primary graph source for the authenticated endpoints build_vertex (chat.py:292/301) and build_vertex_stream (chat.py:418-435), which execute or stream whatever graph is stored under that key.
Impact: an unauthenticated caller who knows (or is given) a flow id can enumerate another user's flow structure and, by posting a crafted `data` body, write an attacker-controlled graph into the process cache under the victim's flow id; a later build/stream of that flow (for example the owner opening it in the playground) then loads and executes the attacker's graph data instead of the stored flow, with the victim's user context.
Fix: add the CurrentActiveUser dependency to this route and verify that the loaded flow's user_id matches the caller before building and caching anything, and key the cache by flow id plus user id so that unauthenticated or foreign writes cannot be consumed by another user's build.

findings.title: Unauthenticated RCE via public flow build endpoint custom code
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:561 (POST /build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow), with the caller-supplied `data` handed to the build at line 614. Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing from anonymous internet user to arbitrary code execution on the Langflow server. Path: the request body `data: FlowDataRequest` (line 567) is passed unchanged to `start_flow_build(data=data)` (line 614) -> `generate_flow_events` (api/build.py:63, 186) -> `create_graph` (api/build.py:253-278), which prefers the request payload over the stored flow (`if not data: build_graph_from_db ... else build_graph_from_data(payload=data.model_dump())`) -> `Graph.from_payload` (api/utils.py:171) -> `graph.build_vertex` (api/build.py:297) -> `Graph.build_vertex` (graph/graph/base.py:1457-1464) -> `Vertex._build` (graph/vertex/base.py:388-391) -> `instantiate_class` (interface/initialize/loading.py:39-40) -> `eval_custom_component_code` -> `validate.create_class` -> `exec(compiled_class, exec_globals, exec_locals)` (utils/validate.py:338). The `code` field of any node in the attacker's payload is compiled and executed, and top-level statements in that module run immediately. Nothing on the path stops it: the only gate is `verify_public_flow_and_get_user` (api/utils.py:324-381), which merely requires that the targeted flow is marked PUBLIC and that a `client_id` cookie is present; it never inspects `data`, never checks ownership of the graph being executed, and there is no allow-list or custom-code restriction, so any public flow id (a common, discoverable resource) is enough. Impact: anonymous remote code execution as the server process - reading environment variables/secrets and the database, and pivoting to other services. Fix: do not accept caller-supplied `data` on the public build endpoint (ignore it or reject the request), or validate it against the stored public flow, and require an authenticated, authorized context before executing custom component code.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller poisons shared graph cache, achieving server-side RCE
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:71 (POST /build/{flow_id}/vertices), where `data: FlowDataRequest` is accepted at line 76. Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing into the shared graph cache used by other users' builds. Path: with `data` supplied, the handler calls `build_and_cache_graph_from_data(flow_id=flow_id, graph_data=data.model_dump(), ...)` (lines 106-108) -> `Graph.from_payload(graph_data, str_flow_id)` and `chat_service.set_cache(str_flow_id, graph)` (api/utils.py:209-210), then caches again at chat.py:116 under the raw `flow_id`. That cache entry is later consumed by the deprecated build route `chat_service.get_cache(flow_id_str)` -> `graph.build_vertex(...)` (chat.py:292-320), which reaches `Vertex._build` -> `instantiate_class` -> `exec` of the attacker's node `code`, and by the unauthenticated `_stream_vertex` (chat.py:418-497, 500-538), which serves the poisoned graph's vertex results. Nothing on the path stops it: `retrieve_vertices_order` has no `CurrentActiveUser` dependency and no ownership check on `flow_id`; `build_and_cache_graph_from_data` performs no validation of the payload; and the cache key is the plain flow id, so any caller can overwrite another user's cached graph with one they control. Impact: stored injection of attacker-authored executable graph data into another user's flow cache - when the flow owner (or any authenticated user) builds a vertex of that flow, the attacker's code executes server-side in that request, and the stream endpoint leaks the poisoned graph's outputs to anonymous callers. Fix: require authentication and verify flow ownership on the vertices route, refuse to build/cache graphs from request-supplied data for flows the caller does not own, and key or validate the cached graph so that a caller can only ever retrieve a graph they are authorized to use.
