Authorization is bypassed for the same actor as well (assertInstanceAdmin at access.ts:1583-1588 and routes/authz.ts:12; assertCompanyAccess at routes/authz.ts:25; assertCompanyPermission at access.ts:1816), and handlers such as promote-instance-admin (2897), join-request approve (2597), reject (2743) and invite revoke (2538) require no request body, so a simple form/fetch POST with a CORS-safelisted content type reaches them without a preflight. Nothing else checks a CSRF token - a repo-wide search finds no csrf middleware. Impact: a malicious page silently promotes an attacker-chosen user id to instance admin, approves a pending join request (onboarding an attacker's agent without the admin's consent) or revokes invites on the user's running instance. Fix: do not exempt local_implicit from the Origin/Referer check (the local UI is served from the same host, so its Origin would match trustedOriginsForRequest), or add a per-session CSRF token / SameSite-protected cookie for all mutating /api routes.

findings.title: Invite holders exhaust server outbound sockets via invite test-resolution probes
findings.description: Entry: server/src/routes/access.ts:2103 (GET /api/invites/:token/test-resolution, url and timeoutMs query params). Attacker: anyone holding a valid, unexpired invite token (an invited-but-untrusted agent/user or anyone given the invite link), crossing the boundary of the server's own outbound network/socket resources. Path: token is looked up at access.ts:2106-2113 (only revoked/expired invites are rejected, so the probe stays usable for the invite's full 10-minute TTL even after acceptance); req.query.url is parsed at 2115-2126 with only an http/https scheme check (no host allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local/metadata block); req.query.timeoutMs is clamped at 2128-2134 to 1-15 seconds; probeInviteResolutionTarget then runs fetch(url, {method: HEAD, redirect: manual, signal}) at 1512-1516. Nothing on the path limits how many probes a caller can start or how long each one holds a connection: there is no rate limit, no concurrency semaphore, and the abort only fires after the attacker-chosen delay (up to 15s). Impact: an invite holder can issue many concurrent test-resolution calls pointing at an unroutable or slow address; each call keeps an outbound socket, a pending fetch and event-loop state alive for up to 15 seconds, so a burst exhausts the server's outbound connection/file-descriptor budget and degrades or stalls legitimate API traffic. Fix: restrict probe targets (deny private, loopback, link-local and cloud-metadata ranges, ideally allowlist expected webhook hosts), add a per-caller rate limit and a global concurrency cap for this endpoint, and use a small fixed probe timeout instead of a caller-supplied one.

findings.title: Non-CEO agent key can export the full company portability bundle via legacy /export
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/companies.ts:165 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/export).
Attacker: a non-CEO agent holding a valid agent API key for the company, crossing the CEO-only boundary the application itself draws for company portability exports.
Path: req.params.companyId and req.body enter the handler; validate(companyPortabilityExportSchema) only validates the payload shape; assertCompanyAccess(req, companyId) passes for any agent whose req.actor.companyId equals the company (middleware/auth.ts sets companyId from the agent API key) and for any board member with a membership; portability.exportBundle(companyId, req.body) is then called with no actor or role argument, so no role check happens anywhere on the path.
Why nothing stops it: the sibling routes POST /:companyId/exports/preview (line 203) and POST /:companyId/exports (line 210) both call assertCanManagePortability(req, companyId, "exports"), which throws unless the acting agent is the company CEO, and PATCH /:companyId/branding likewise requires the CEO role; the legacy /export route was left with the weaker company-membership check, so a general (non-CEO) agent key that the codebase deliberately denies on /exports can still obtain the full portable bundle through /export.
Impact: a low-privileged agent credential can exfiltrate the entire company portability bundle (company settings, agents and their adapter configuration, projects, issues and related records), which the application restricts to CEO agents.
Fix: replace assertCompanyAccess(req, companyId) in the /export handler with await assertCanManagePortability(req, companyId, "exports") (or delete the legacy route) so every export door enforces the same role policy.

findings.title: Agent API key can delete any issue and its attachment objects
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/issues.ts:1960 (DELETE /api/issues/:id).
Attacker: any agent holding a valid agent API key for the company, crossing the board/agent boundary that the same file enforces for other destructive issue operations.
Path: req.params.id is resolved to an issue via router.param and svc.getById; the handler then calls only assertCompanyAccess(req, existing.companyId) (which for agent actors just compares req.actor.companyId with the issue's company) and proceeds straight to svc.remove(id) plus storage.deleteObject for every attachment; there is no assertBoard, no permission-key check (such as tasks:assign used for assignment), and no per-actor ownership check.
Why nothing stops it: sibling destructive handlers in the same router are stricter, e.g. DELETE /issues/:id/documents/:key rejects non-board actors at line 1004 and POST/DELETE /issues/:id/read and /issues/:id/inbox-archive require req.actor.type === "board" at lines 1132, 1196 and 1228, so the codebase does distinguish board-only mutations; the delete route simply omits that check, and no service-level authorization compensates because issueService.remove takes only the issue id.
Impact: an automation credential can irreversibly destroy arbitrary issues and their attachment objects in its company (audit/activity history is written only after the deletion), which is a capability reserved for board users elsewhere in this file.
Fix: require board authentication (assertBoard(req), optionally gated on an instance-admin or explicit permission key) before svc.remove in this handler, matching the document-delete route.

findings.title: Hard-coded embedded PostgreSQL credentials give any local user superuser access
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/index.ts:351 and 371-375 (embedded PostgreSQL startup when no DATABASE_URL is set), whose credentials are reused at index.ts:413 and index.ts:419.
Attacker: any other local user or process on the same host (or in a container sharing the loopback interface) that can reach the embedded database port, crossing from "local unprivileged process" into the application's database and secret store.
Path: when DATABASE_URL is unset, the server starts EmbeddedPostgres with user: "paperclip" and password: "paperclip" and then builds the admin and application connection strings as postgres://paperclip:paperclip@127.0.0.1:<port>/... ; the same literal is compiled into the published package, so the credential is readable by anyone who reads the source and is identical on every deployment.
Nothing on the path stops it: the password is a fixed literal with no per-installation randomisation and no 0600 file like the secrets master key uses (server/src/secrets/local-encrypted-provider.ts:63-72); the database trusts password authentication, so a local attacker can connect as the superuser account, read/write every table including auth users, sessions, board API key hashes, company secret ciphertext and the verification records, and can insert rows to mint their own identity.
Impact: total compromise of the instance's stored identities and secrets from a local foothold, without needing any application-level credential.
Fix: generate a random password on first initialisation, persist it in a 0600 file alongside the data directory (or require an operator-supplied DATABASE_URL), and never ship a literal credential in source.

findings.title: Stored XSS: uploaded HTML asset served inline from app origin
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/assets.ts:110 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/assets/images), upload stored and later served by server/src/routes/assets.ts:312 (GET /api/assets/:assetId/content).
Attacker: any authenticated user or agent key that has access to a company, crossing into the browser session/origin of another user of that company, including an instance admin.
Path: the multipart file's client-supplied MIME type goes to assets.ts:141-145, where the SVG special-case is skipped for non-SVG types and isAllowedContentType() is called; server/src/attachment-types.ts:18-30 puts text/html in DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TYPES and matchesContentType() accepts it exactly, so an HTML file is stored. On retrieval, assets.ts:322-331 sets Content-Type from the stored value, adds no Content-Security-Policy unless the type is exactly image/svg+xml (line 327), and always sends Content-Disposition: inline (line 331).
Nothing stops it: the allow-list check is the only gate and it deliberately admits text/html, the response is served with that exact Content-Type, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff does not prevent rendering a correctly typed HTML document, and the sandbox CSP is applied only to SVG. An attacker who is merely a member of a company can send the resulting /api/assets/<id>/content link to another member or to an instance admin (admins can access every company, so assertCompanyAccess passes for them), and the HTML runs as a same-origin document with the victim's session, letting it call every API the victim can call, including instance-admin routes.
Impact: stored XSS in the application origin, usable for privilege escalation from a low-privileged company member to instance admin and for reading/altering all data the victim can reach.
Fix: remove text/html (and other active types) from DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TYPES, and in the asset content handler always send Content-Disposition: attachment for anything that is not a raster image, or send a strict sandbox CSP for every non-image content type instead of only for the exact image/svg+xml string.

findings.title: Stored XSS via SVG attachment whose MIME parameters bypass the sandbox CSP
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/issues.ts:2632 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/issues/:issueId/attachments), served by server/src/routes/issues.ts:2719 (GET /api/attachments/:attachmentId/content).
Attacker: any authenticated user or agent key with access to a company, crossing into another user's browser session in the application origin (including an instance admin who opens the attachment link).
Path: the multipart part's MIME type is taken verbatim at issues.ts:2665 via normalizeContentType() with no isAllowedContentType() check anywhere on this route (the only callers of that function are in assets.ts), and the raw bytes are stored. At retrieval, issues.ts:2729-2730 sets Content-Type to the stored string, issues.ts:2738 decides inline vs attachment through isInlineAttachmentContentType(), which matches by prefix ("image/*" matches "image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8"), while issues.ts:2734 applies the sandbox CSP only when responseContentType === "image/svg+xml" by exact string equality.
Nothing stops it: uploading an SVG with the part Content-Type "image/svg+xml; charset=utf-8" (a valid MIME type a Blob/FormData can carry) stores that exact string; the prefix match makes it inline, the exact-equality CSP check fails so no sandbox header is sent, and the browser renders the SVG document and executes its script. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff does not help because the declared type is a legitimate SVG type. An attacker who is a member of the company only needs to get another member or an instance admin to open the returned contentPath.
Impact: stored XSS in the application origin from a low-privileged company member to any user with access to that company, enabling session-wide API calls, secret management, and instance-admin actions as the victim.
Fix: enforce an explicit allow-list on attachment uploads, and in the content handler parse the media type (strip parameters) before both the inline decision and the CSP check, applying the sandbox CSP to all SVG types (and serving everything that is not a raster image as an attachment).

findings.title: Authenticated user can OOM shared server via unbounded GitHub import fetches
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/companies.ts:217 (router.post("/:companyId/imports/preview", validate(companyPortabilityPreviewSchema)) -> portability.previewImport(req.body) at line 226; the same path is reachable from companies.ts:172 POST /import/preview and companies.ts:233 imports/apply).
Attacker: any authenticated board user who is a member of a company (or a CEO agent on the agent-safe route), crossing the boundary of their own tenant by consuming the shared Node process's memory and outbound bandwidth, which can take the server down for every other tenant.
Path: req.body.source is parsed by portabilitySourceSchema (packages/shared/src/validators/company-portability.ts:185-187) as { type: "github", url: z.string().url() } with no host restriction; resolveSource (company-portability.ts:2751) calls parseGitHubSourceUrl (2690-2738) which checks only url.protocol === "https:" and then keeps url.hostname verbatim; the hostname flows into gitHubApiBase/resolveRawGitHubUrl (server/src/services/github-fetch.ts:8-17) and then into fetchJson/fetchText (company-portability.ts:2791, 2812, 2823) -> ghFetch (github-fetch.ts:19-25) -> response.json()/response.text(). Lines 2795-2808 build candidatePaths from every blob in the remote recursive tree with no cap on the count, and 2809-2815 issues one full-body fetch per path, storing every body in the single in-memory `files` record; fetchBinary at 2833 does the same with arrayBuffer() for the logo.
Nothing on the path stops it: ghFetch is a bare fetch with no AbortSignal and no timeout, fetchText/fetchOptionalText/fetchBinary/fetchJson (2187-2222) never inspect Content-Length or stream-abort on a size threshold, there is no per-file or total-byte budget and no limit on how many blobs are downloaded, and the only inbound protection is express.json({ limit: "10mb" }) (server/src/app.ts:118-124) which bounds the request body, not the size of the outbound responses. The private-hostname guard (app.ts:132-138) only gates the inbound Host header, and assertBoard/assertCanManagePortability (companies.ts:76-88, 217-231) check authorization, not cost.
Impact: a request of a few hundred bytes can make the server download an unbounded number of unbounded remote files (the attacker simply serves, or selects, a GitHub/GHE repository with a huge tree and huge .md files), holding all of it in one process; repeated or concurrent requests exhaust memory and OOM-kill the server, and the JSON parsing/manifest building over all of that content blocks the single event loop, denying service to all tenants.
Fix: allow-list the fetch host (github.com and the configured GHE hostname only) instead of trusting url.hostname, and re-validate after DNS resolution; give ghFetch an AbortSignal timeout and a maximum byte budget; stream each response and abort once a per-file and per-request total cap is exceeded; reject or truncate responses whose Content-Length exceeds the cap; and bound the number of tree entries fetched (and the size of the tree JSON itself).

findings.title: Cross-tenant secret disclosure via plugin secret-ref resolution
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1542 (POST /api/plugins/:pluginId/config, guarded only by assertBoard; the resolve RPC itself is server/src/services/plugin-secrets-handler.ts:261).
Attacker: an authenticated board user who is a member of company A only, crossing the per-company boundary to obtain the plaintext of company B's secret.
Path: the caller POSTs /api/plugins/:pluginId/config with configJson containing company B's secret UUID (as a declared format:"secret-ref" field, or as any UUID-shaped string when the plugin declares no instanceConfigSchema — extractSecretRefsFromConfig falls back to collecting every UUID, lines 122-162). The config is persisted instance-wide by plugin-registry.upsertConfig (no company scoping). When the plugin worker calls ctx.secrets.resolve(secretRef), the handler accepts the ref because it is now in cachedAllowedRefs (lines 289-309), then queries companySecrets with only eq(companySecrets.id, trimmedRef) (lines 314-318) — no companyId predicate — fetches the latest version material (lines 327-336) and returns provider.resolveVersion(...) plaintext (lines 345-351).
Why nothing stops it: the config route never calls assertCompanyAccess (plugin config is instance-wide), and the handler has no company parameter at all; it never compares secret.companyId to any company the caller belongs to. Every other secret path in this codebase (services/secrets.ts assertSecretInCompany, routines resolveTriggerSecret) enforces that match; this path deliberately omits it. The rate limiter, UUID format check and 30s config cache do not constrain which company the UUID belongs to.
Impact: cross-tenant secret disclosure. A user with access to one company can make any installed plugin with the secrets.read-ref capability resolve arbitrary other companies' secrets, and any plugin that uses a configured secret in an outbound request whose URL/headers are also attacker-controlled config values lets the attacker exfiltrate the plaintext. This bypasses the per-company restriction enforced on /companies/:companyId/secrets.
Fix: pass the acting company into createPluginSecretsHandler and require the resolved secret's companyId to be one the plugin is allowed to act for (or the caller's accessible companies); additionally require instance-admin for writing plugin config and/or for secret-ref fields, and validate that every secret UUID written into plugin config belongs to a company the caller can access.</br>

findings.title: Unsalted SHA-256 of every secret value enables offline cracking from DB dumps
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/secrets.ts:39 (POST /companies/:companyId/secrets), with the same path on POST /secrets/:id/rotate at server/src/routes/secrets.ts:69.
Attacker: a party who obtains read access to the secrets database or a database backup/replica (the DB is exactly the party the at-rest encryption does not trust), crossing the boundary AES-256-GCM encryption is supposed to draw between stored data and the plaintext secret values.
Path: the request body value passes validate(createSecretSchema) (or rotateSecretSchema), then secretService.create (server/src/services/secrets.ts:184) or rotate (:227) calls provider.createVersion, where localEncryptedProvider computes valueSha256: sha256Hex(input.value) at server/src/secrets/local-encrypted-provider.ts:127 using an unsalted, unkeyed, single-round SHA-256 (sha256Hex at line 75). services/secrets.ts then persists it into company_secret_versions.value_sha256 on every version insert (line 209 for create, line 237 for rotate), and packages/db/src/schema/company_secret_versions.ts:12/20 stores it as a NOT NULL, btree-indexed column.
Why nothing stops it: no guard, salt, key, iteration count, or KDF is applied anywhere on this path; the master key that protects the ciphertext is never used for this digest, and a grep of the whole repository shows valueSha256 is written but never read by any code, so the column has no functional purpose that would justify its exposure.
Impact: an attacker with only DB access (dump, backup, replica, or SQL access gained through another flaw) gets an offline verifier for every stored secret. Low-entropy values such as passwords, shared webhook secrets, and short tokens can be brute-forced cheaply, and any guessed value can be confirmed against the indexed hash; because the hash is unsalted and global, identical secret values are also linkable across companies and versions. This defeats the entire point of encrypting values with AES-256-GCM at rest.
Fix: stop computing and storing valueSha256 (drop the column and its index, since nothing reads it), or if an equality check is genuinely required, store a keyed HMAC-SHA-256 (or HKDF-derived subkey) of the value under the secrets master key so that a database-only attacker learns nothing and cross-tenant equality cannot be tested.

findings.title: Authenticated user can stall whole instance via unbounded adapterConfig.env bindings
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/agents.ts:833 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/adapters/:type/test-environment), which passes the caller-supplied body.adapterConfig into normalizeAdapterConfigForPersistence and then resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime (server/src/routes/agents.ts:838).
Attacker: an authenticated board user who holds only the agents:create permission on one company (assertCanReadConfigurations -> assertCanCreateAgentsForCompany, server/src/routes/agents.ts:234-249 and 827), crossing the tenant boundary by consuming instance-wide CPU, database connections and the single Node event loop that every other company shares.
Path: req.body.adapterConfig.env (a plain JSON object, bounded only by express.json's 10mb limit) -> normalizeAdapterConfigForPersistenceInternal (services/secrets.ts:151) -> normalizeEnvConfig, whose loop at services/secrets.ts:108 iterates every key of that object and calls assertSecretInCompany (services/secrets.ts:76-81) -> getById -> one SELECT per key; then resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime (services/secrets.ts:360-375) iterates the same keys again and calls resolveSecretValue (services/secrets.ts:83-97) -> assertSecretInCompany (another SELECT) + getSecretVersion (a second SELECT) + localEncryptedProvider.resolveVersion -> loadOrCreateMasterKey, which does a synchronous readFileSync of the master key on every single resolution (server/src/secrets/local-encrypted-provider.ts:53-55, 131-134) plus an AES-GCM decrypt.
Nothing on the path stops it: ENV_KEY_RE and envBindingSchema validate the shape of each entry but never the number of entries; assertSecretInCompany throws only for a secret that does not exist in the company, and the same valid secretId can be repeated for an unlimited number of distinct keys, so one self-created secret is enough to drive the loop; the 10mb body limit still admits roughly 100k+ secret_ref entries of ~50-90 bytes each; there is no per-request binding cap and no batching. One HTTP request therefore turns into ~300k sequential database round trips plus ~100k synchronous master-key file reads, all awaited on the single Node event loop.
Impact for this application: the server process stalls for minutes on one request (synchronous fs reads and sequential awaits block every other request, including other companies'), the Postgres connection pool is saturated, and the load is trivially repeatable in parallel, so a member of one company can take the whole instance offline.
Fix: cap the number of entries accepted in an env object (e.g. 100) and reject larger ones with 422 before any lookup; resolve bindings with a single batched query (WHERE secret_id = ANY(...)) instead of one query per key; cache the decoded master key in memory once per process instead of readFileSync per resolution; and enforce the cap in normalizeEnvConfig, resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime and resolveEnvBindings so every caller inherits it.

findings.title: HTTP adapter lets any tenant user SSRF the server into internal networks
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/agents.ts:1870 (PATCH /api/agents/:id, adapterConfig.url) and server/src/routes/agents.ts:1487 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/agents), consumed at server/src/services/heartbeat.ts:3677 via getServerAdapter(agent.adapterType).execute.
Attacker: any user with access to the company (board actor; assertCanUpdateAgent at routes/agents.ts:318-320 only checks company access) or an agent key acting on its own agent record (same function returns immediately when actorAgent.id === targetAgent.id), crossing from tenant/agent scope into the server host's internal network.
Path: adapterConfig.url -> svc.create/svc.update -> agent row -> heartbeat resolves it (resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime) -> adapter.execute({config}) -> `const url = asString(config.url, "")` (execute.ts:6) -> `fetch(url, { method, headers, body: JSON.stringify({...payloadTemplate, agentId, runId, context}) })` (execute.ts:19-27).
Why nothing stops it: the only checks on this path are `if (!url) throw` and the free-form adapterConfig record validator (packages/shared/src/validators/agent.ts:34, which only inspects `env`); there is no scheme allow-list, no host allow-list, no private/loopback/link-local check and no DNS pinning before the fetch, and `fetch` follows redirects by default so an external URL can bounce the POST to an internal one. The repository does contain exactly this defence for plugin HTTP fetches (isPrivateIP + validateAndResolveFetchUrl in server/src/services/plugin-host-services.ts:60-176), but the HTTP adapter never calls it.
Impact: the Paperclip server issues attacker-shaped requests (arbitrary method, headers such as Metadata-Flavor, arbitrary JSON body built from payloadTemplate plus run context) into loopback, RFC1918 and 169.254.169.254 endpoints, i.e. state-changing blind SSRF against internal admin APIs and cloud metadata services from a tenant-scoped caller, with run telemetry/logs leaking the target URL.
Fix: validate `config.url` before fetching - allow only http/https, resolve the hostname and reject loopback/private/link-local/ULA/0.0.0.0 and IPv4-mapped IPv6 (reuse isPrivateIP/validateAndResolveFetchUrl from plugin-host-services.ts), pin the resolved IP for the connection, set `redirect: "manual"` (or re-validate every redirect hop), and offer an operator-configured host allow-list for the http adapter.

findings.title: Cross-tenant data read via plugin bridge params.companyId
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:795 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/bridge/data")), authorization check at 829-831, worker call at 834-842.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A crossing into company B's data (cross-tenant IDOR).
The handler validates only the top-level body.companyId with assertCompanyAccess, then forwards body.params verbatim to the plugin worker's getData RPC. Plugin handlers read the company scope from params.companyId (the documented SDK pattern: packages/plugins/sdk/src/ui/hooks.ts:28-33 passes {companyId: context.companyId} in params, and the bundled example packages/plugins/examples/plugin-kitchen-sink-example/src/worker.ts:221 does `const companyId = typeof params.companyId === "string" ? params.companyId : ""` and then `ctx.issues.list({ companyId })`), and the host services those calls reach (plugin-host-services.ts:441) execute with the plugin's capabilities and no caller identity, so they return the requested company's issues/goals/agents. A caller therefore sends {companyId: "<company they belong to>", params: {companyId: "<victim company>"}}; the check passes on the first field while the plugin acts on the second. If the top-level companyId is simply omitted (line 829 is an `if`), assertCompanyAccess never runs at all.
Impact: any member of any company can read another company's issues, goals, agents and projects through any installed plugin that follows the documented handler pattern.
Fix: derive the company scope server-side (from the resolved plugin/actor) and pass it to the worker, rejecting any params.companyId that does not match the authorized company; make the company parameter mandatory rather than optional.

findings.title: Authenticated user can mutate another company's records via plugin bridge action params
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:878 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/bridge/action")), authorization check at 912-914, worker call at 916-925.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A crossing into company B's data and mutating it.
Same defect as the bridge/data route but on the write path: only body.companyId is checked with assertCompanyAccess, while body.params is forwarded untouched to the worker's performAction RPC, and plugin handlers take the company from params.companyId (packages/plugins/examples/plugin-kitchen-sink-example/src/worker.ts:478-508 uses getCurrentCompanyId(params) and then ctx.issues.create({ companyId, ... }) / ctx.issues.update(issueId, ..., companyId)). Nothing between the route and the host service re-checks the caller's membership, and the check is skipped entirely when body.companyId is absent.
Impact: a member of one company can create or modify records in another company (and trigger any other privileged plugin action) by supplying the victim company inside params.
Fix: resolve the acting company server-side, require it, and reject any params.companyId that differs from the authorized company before dispatching to the worker.

findings.title: Cross-tenant data read via unvalidated params.companyId in plugin getData proxy
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:962 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/data/:key")), authorization check at 995-997, worker call at 1000-1008.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A reading company B's data through a plugin (cross-tenant IDOR).
Identical to POST /plugins/:pluginId/bridge/data: the handler calls assertCompanyAccess on body.companyId only if it is present, then forwards body.params unchanged to the getData RPC, where plugin handlers resolve the company from params.companyId and query the host services with it. The top-level companyId can be omitted (skipping the check) or set to the attacker's own company while params.companyId names the victim.
Impact: any authenticated user can pull another company's issues/goals/agents/projects out of any installed plugin that follows the documented params.companyId convention.
Fix: compute the authorized company server-side and overwrite/validate params.companyId before the RPC instead of trusting the client-provided fields.

findings.title: Cross-company plugin actions via unvalidated companyId in params
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1041 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/actions/:key")), authorization check at 1074-1076, worker call at 1079-1088.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A performing actions against company B's data.
The URL-keyed action route mirrors /bridge/action: assertCompanyAccess runs against body.companyId (and is skipped when that field is absent), while the worker's performAction handler reads the company from body.params (getCurrentCompanyId(params) in the bundled example) and then writes through host services that carry only the plugin's capabilities, not the caller's memberships.
Impact: cross-company writes and privileged plugin actions driven by any authenticated user of any company.
Fix: derive and enforce the acting company on the server, and reject params that name a different company.

findings.title: Board user can spoof agent identity to run agent-only plugin tools
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:519 (router.post("/plugins/tools/execute")), validation at 546-553, dispatch at 563-567.
Attacker: an authenticated board user crossing the agent boundary — executing plugin-contributed agent tools under a fabricated agent identity (agentId/runId chosen by the caller).
The whole runContext (agentId, runId, companyId, projectId) comes from the request body; the only authorization performed is assertCompanyAccess(req, runContext.companyId) (line 553), which merely proves the caller belongs to that company. Nothing verifies that agentId is an agent of that company, that it is not terminated/pending_approval, or that runId is a run of that agent; plugin-tool-dispatcher.ts:396-414 passes the object straight to the plugin registry/worker, where the plugin's tool handler treats runContext.agentId as the trusted caller identity. A board user who is only a member of company X can therefore invoke agent-only plugin tools as any agent of X (or of any company they can reach) and any audit/authorization decision a plugin makes on runContext.agentId is attacker-controlled.
Impact: agent-identity spoofing and invocation of plugin tools outside their intended agent-run context, defeating any per-agent restriction a plugin implements from runContext.
Fix: when the caller is a board actor, ignore the client-supplied agentId/runId (or require them to match a real, active agent of the authorized company and an existing run), and never treat request-body identity fields as authoritative inside plugin tool handlers.

findings.title: Any board user can read and overwrite instance-wide plugin secrets
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1542 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/config")), devUiUrl strip at 1561-1566, upsert at 1583-1585; the read twin is GET /plugins/:pluginId/config at 1512-1524.
Attacker: any authenticated board user (a company member with no instance-admin role) crossing into instance-level plugin secrets and configuration.
The route only calls assertBoard, then persists the caller-supplied configJson verbatim through registry.upsertConfig. The code itself acknowledges that board-level users are not trusted here — it strips devUiUrl for non-instance-admins because it "could be abused for SSRF" (comment at 1558-1560) — yet every other field, including secret values (API tokens, webhook signing secrets) that plugins rely on, is writable by any logged-in user; GET /plugins/:pluginId/config then returns the stored configJson to that same caller. Plugins are instance-global, and comparable instance-wide mutations require instance admin (authz.ts:10, instance-settings.ts:9-17).
Impact: a non-admin member of any company can read and exfiltrate instance-wide plugin credentials, or point a plugin's configuration at an attacker-controlled endpoint so its next run leaks data, without ever being an instance administrator.
Fix: require assertInstanceAdmin for plugin config reads and writes (at minimum for keys that hold secrets), or mark secret fields write-only and never return their values to non-admin callers.

findings.title: Authenticated user uploads HTML asset served inline, enabling stored XSS
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/assets.ts:110 (POST /companies/:companyId/assets/images), content-type decision at line 141.
Attacker: any authenticated user or agent with access to the company, crossing the boundary from "can upload an image asset" to "can store script-capable HTML that is later served from the application origin" (the endpoint is named assets/images and its logo sibling only accepts image/*).
Path: multer parses the multipart part and exposes the client-declared Content-Type as file.mimetype (line 128); line 141 lowercases it and line 142 accepts it whenever isAllowedContentType returns true; that function matches against DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TYPES (server/src/attachment-types.ts:18-30, 84-91), which includes text/html, application/json and text/* by default, so a file declared as text/html is accepted and the raw HTML body is stored (line 146-167) with contentType = "text/html". The UI (ui/src/api/assets.ts:5-19) passes the browser's file.type straight through, so no client-side restriction compensates either.
Why nothing stops it: the MIME type is fully client-controlled and is never cross-checked against the bytes or the file extension (no magic-byte sniffing, no image decoding), and the default allow-list shipped in the code contains text/html; an operator only avoids this by explicitly overriding PAPERCLIP_ALLOWED_ATTACHMENT_TYPES. The only special handling is for image/svg+xml (sanitized at lines 147-154), while HTML is stored unchanged.
Impact: any company member or agent can plant an HTML document in the company's asset store; combined with the inline serving of GET /assets/:assetId/content (lines 322-331) this becomes stored XSS in the application origin and privilege escalation into the session of higher-privileged users who open the asset, and it also lets non-image content be presented as an image asset to every company member.
Fix: on this endpoint validate that the file is actually an image (magic-byte/decoder check) and reject anything outside an explicit image allow-list; stop using the environment-expandable attachment allow-list here and remove text/html and other script-capable types from the defaults used for inline-served assets.

cases.checks: Of 1 published vulnerability in mlflow/mlflow@083eac9c, how many does a scan capped at $3 report?

detail.what: GHSA-7QHF-V65M-G5F3 (authz) MLflow FastAPI Jobs端点完全绕过认证鉴权（CWE-306） - __init__.py

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers bypass auth on FastAPI routes to read, submit, and cancel jobs
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:2949 (fastapi_permission_middleware). Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller crossing the login boundary, reaching routes that require a valid MLflow account. Path: the request hits the FastAPI app built by create_fastapi_app (mlflow/server/fastapi_app.py:61), which includes job_api_router (/ajax-api/3.0/jobs, mlflow/server/job_api.py:15) and otel_router before mounting Flask at "/"; the middleware runs _find_fastapi_validator(path) (line 2910), which returns a validator only when path.startswith("/gateway/"), and for every other FastAPI-native route validator is None, so line 2959 returns `await call_next(request)` without calling _authenticate_request (line 2973) and without checking any Authorization header. Flask's _before_request (line 1746), which authenticates every non-static route, is never invoked because these routers are matched before the WSGI mount. Nothing on the path stops it: job_api.py imports no auth dependency and its endpoints (get_job, submit_job, cancel_job, search_jobs) return job_name, params (including experiment ids and job arguments), result and status; the OTLP export endpoint likewise has no dependency. Impact: an anonymous caller can enumerate and read all server jobs, submit new jobs on the server's job executor, cancel running jobs, and write traces through the OTLP endpoint, with none of the basic-auth or workspace/permission checks that protect the equivalent REST routes. Fix: authenticate and default-deny before the validator lookup (call _authenticate_request first, return 401 when the user is None), or give every FastAPI-native route an explicit validator so that an unmatched path is rejected rather than passed through.

findings.title: Authenticated user can invoke scorers and gateway endpoints without permission
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:1595 ("(INVOKE_SCORER, POST): validate_gateway_proxy"; the same validator is bound to GATEWAY_PROXY at 1593-1594). Attacker: an authenticated MLflow user who has no permission on the target experiment or gateway endpoint, crossing the per-experiment/per-endpoint authorization boundary. Path: POST /ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke with body {"experiment_id": ..., "serialized_scorer": ..., "trace_ids": [...]} reaches _before_request (line 1746), which finds validate_gateway_proxy in BEFORE_REQUEST_VALIDATORS and calls it; validate_gateway_proxy returns True unconditionally (line 1419), so no permission lookup happens. The handler _invoke_scorer_handler (mlflow/server/handlers.py:5110) then takes experiment_id, serialized_scorer and trace_ids straight from the request body, calls get_trace_batches_for_scorer to fetch the traces, and submits scorer jobs, with no experiment, scorer or workspace permission check anywhere in the handler. Nothing on the path stops it: every sibling scorer route (RegisterScorer, GetScorer, DeleteScorer, the scorer permission routes) is bound to validate_can_update_experiment / validate_can_read_scorer / validate_can_manage_scorer_permission, so this is the one scorer operation with no guard; the same always-true validator also removes the per-endpoint USE check (_validate_gateway_use_permission) that the FastAPI /gateway routes enforce, letting any authenticated user invoke arbitrary gateway endpoints through the Flask proxy. Impact: a user with no rights on an experiment can read its traces through scorer evaluation, write assessments into it, and consume server/LLM compute; the same applies to invoking gateway endpoints they were not granted USE on. Fix: bind INVOKE_SCORER to a validator that resolves the experiment_id from the body and requires at least read/update (or scorer manage) permission on that experiment, and bind GATEWAY_PROXY to a validator that resolves the endpoint name and requires USE permission instead of returning True.

findings.title: Authenticated user can enumerate all model versions via GraphQL
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/handlers.py:3331 (the /graphql route, registered at handlers.py:5237). Attacker: any authenticated non-admin user (e.g. a user with no grant on a registered model, or a user in another workspace), crossing the per-object authorization boundary enforced by the basic-auth permission system. Path: the caller POSTs {"query": "{ mlflowSearchModelVersions(input: {}) { model_versions { name version source run_id } } }"} to /graphql; handlers._graphql parses it and executes the schema with GraphQLAuthorizationMiddleware. In resolve() (auth/__init__.py:2702-2705) field_name is "mlflowSearchModelVersions", which is not in PROTECTED_FIELDS, so next(root, info, **args) is invoked without any permission check, and QueryType.resolve_mlflow_search_model_versions (mlflow/server/graphql/autogenerated_graphql_schema.py:332-336) calls mlflow.server.handlers.search_model_versions_impl directly. Nothing on the path stops it: the only other gate for /graphql is authentication in _before_request (auth/__init__.py:1750-1767), and _find_validator returns None because /graphql is not in BEFORE_REQUEST_VALIDATORS, so the per-field middleware is the sole authorization layer; search_model_versions_impl performs no permission filtering and there is no after-request filtering for GraphQL. Impact: any logged-in user can enumerate every registered model version in every workspace (names, versions, source URIs, run ids, tags, descriptions) even when the deployment relies on default_permission=NO_PERMISSIONS or workspace isolation. Fix: add "mlflowSearchModelVersions" to PROTECTED_FIELDS and, for that field, resolve each returned model version's registered model and enforce read permission (returning only readable ones), also covering the nested MlflowRunExtension.resolve_model_versions field.

findings.title: Shipped default admin password (admin/password1234) grants full admin access
findings.description:
Entry: mlflow/server/auth/basic_auth.ini:5 (loaded by mlflow/server/auth/config.py:23 when MLFLOW_AUTH_CONFIG_PATH is unset, seeded by mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:3046).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller who has read the public repository, crossing the login and administrator boundary.
The path: read_auth_config() falls back to this committed file, create_app() calls create_admin_user(auth_config.admin_username, auth_config.admin_password), which calls store.create_user(username, password, is_admin=True), so the account admin/password1234 is created on first startup.
Nothing on the path stops it: the fallback to the in-repo file is unconditional, the code never requires the operator to override the password or detects the placeholder, and the value is committed to the repository so it is public.
Impact: every deployment started with `mlflow server --app-name basic-auth` that does not point MLFLOW_AUTH_CONFIG_PATH at its own config has a fully privileged administrator account whose password anyone can look up; the attacker can log in, create users, grant themselves permissions on all experiments and models, read all data, and change the admin password.
Fix: do not ship a default password; require admin_password (or the admin user itself) to be supplied via configuration/environment and fail startup if it is missing or still the placeholder, or generate a random one-time password at first startup and force a change.

findings.title: HEAD requests bypass gateway path allow-list and proxy arbitrary paths
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/__init__.py:143 registers /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/gateway-proxy with methods=["POST", "GET"] and dispatches to gateway_proxy_handler (mlflow/server/handlers.py:2030). Attacker: any client that can reach the tracking server (the basic-auth plugin exempts this route from all permission checks via validate_gateway_proxy at mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:1414-1419), crossing the gateway-path allow-list that is supposed to limit which paths the server proxies to MLFLOW_DEPLOYMENTS_TARGET. Path: because the route allows GET, Werkzeug automatically adds HEAD, and Flask dispatches HEAD to the same view with request.method == "HEAD". Line 2036 therefore takes args = request.json (method is not "GET"), letting the caller supply gateway_path and json_data in the body. _validate_gateway_path (handlers.py:2008-2026) has branches only for method == "GET" (exact match "api/2.0/endpoints") and method == "POST" (regex gateway/[^/]+/invocations); for method == "HEAD" only the non-empty check runs, so any gateway_path value passes. Line 2040 then executes requests.request("HEAD", f"{target_uri}/{gateway_path}", json=json_data) against the deployments service at an attacker-chosen path with an attacker-chosen JSON body. Nothing on the path stops this: the route has no auth guard, and the only input restriction is keyed on the request-method string, which the HEAD alias evades. The target host is fixed by operator configuration, so this is not arbitrary-host SSRF, but it defeats the code's own path allow-list and turns the tracking server into a blind request proxy/oracle against the deployments service (the non-200 status is echoed in the raised MlflowException message; a 200 response makes response.json() fail on the empty HEAD body). Fix: in _validate_gateway_path, explicitly reject any method other than GET and POST (add an else/elif branch raising INVALID_PARAMETER_VALUE), or check request.method against an explicit allow-list in gateway_proxy_handler before building the URL.

findings.title: Authenticated user can read any experiment's trace artifact via 3.0 endpoint
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/__init__.py:157 (@app.route(_add_static_prefix("/ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/get-trace-artifact"))). Attacker: an authenticated user with no permission on the target experiment/workspace, crossing the per-experiment authorization boundary. The request hits get_trace_artifact_handler with an arbitrary request_id; the handler fetches the trace (or its artifact repo) and streams the trace data without any permission lookup. The authorization layer only maps the 2.0 path: mlflow/server/auth/routes.py:32 defines GET_TRACE_ARTIFACT with _get_ajax_path's default version=2, so BEFORE_REQUEST_VALIDATORS contains only ("/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/get-trace-artifact", "GET") (mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:1588). _find_validator does an exact dict lookup, the path is not a /mlflow/logged-models path, and _is_proxy_artifact_path is false, so no validator runs for the 3.0 route; only basic authentication is enforced. The frontend itself calls this 3.0 endpoint (mlflow/server/js/src/experiment-tracking/pages/experiment-scorers/useEvaluateTraces.common.ts:11), so it is reachable in practice, and any authenticated low-privilege user can read traces of any experiment by guessing request_id. Fix: register the 3.0 path in BEFORE_REQUEST_VALIDATORS with validate_can_read_trace_artifact (or make _find_validator match version-agnostic routes), and add a defense-in-depth permission check inside get_trace_artifact_handler.

findings.title: Authenticated user can download any logged model's artifacts via model_id
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/__init__.py:162-167 (@app.route(_add_static_prefix("/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/logged-models/<model_id>/artifacts/files"))). Attacker: an authenticated user with no permission on the logged model's experiment/workspace, crossing the per-experiment authorization boundary. get_logged_model_artifact_handler loads the logged model by the client-supplied model_id and streams the requested artifact file (_send_artifact) without checking the caller's experiment or workspace permission. The auth layer does not cover this route: _find_validator special-cases any path containing "/mlflow/logged-models" and returns next((v for (pat, method), v in LOGGED_MODEL_BEFORE_REQUEST_VALIDATORS.items() if pat.fullmatch(req.path) and method == req.method), None) (mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:1701-1711), and LOGGED_MODEL_BEFORE_REQUEST_VALIDATORS is built from proto service endpoints via get_endpoints (mlflow/server/handlers.py:5226-5247), which does not include this manually registered Flask route. A repository-wide search shows "/artifacts/files" appears only in mlflow/server/__init__.py and the JS client, so no validator ever matches, _find_validator returns None, and _before_request performs no authorization check at all (only authentication). Result: any valid low-privilege account can download artifacts of any logged model by model_id, including models in other experiments/workspaces. Fix: register this route with a validator that resolves the logged model's experiment (or workspace) and requires READ permission, mirroring _get_permission_from_model_id, and re-check it in get_logged_model_artifact_handler.

findings.title: Unauthenticated negative max_results triggers unbounded metric query (DoS)
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/__init__.py:120 (/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/metrics/get-history-bulk) -> get_metric_history_bulk_handler. Attacker: an unauthenticated network client of a default MLflow tracking server (no auth is enabled unless MLFLOW_AUTH_CONFIG_PATH is set), crossing the boundary between a trivial request and unbounded server-side query work. Path: request.args["max_results"] is parsed with int() and only clamped on the high side by min(max_results, MAX_HISTORY_RESULTS); there is no lower-bound check, so max_results=-1 (or any negative value) is passed unchanged to store.get_metric_history_bulk(run_ids=..., metric_key=..., max_results=-1) (mlflow/store/tracking/sqlalchemy_store.py:1322-1357). SQLAlchemy emits `.limit(-1)` and SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as "no upper bound", so the query returns every metric row for the key across the requested runs (up to 100 run_ids are allowed); on other SQL backends the negative limit surfaces as an unhandled DB error. The handler then serializes all rows and returns `metrics_with_run_ids[:max_results]`, and the slice `[: -1]` drops only the last element, so nearly the entire unbounded result set is returned. Nothing else on the path validates the parameter: unlike the sibling get_metric_history_bulk_interval_handler (line 1915-1923, which enforces 1..MAX_RESULTS_PER_RUN), this handler has no schema at all. Impact: one small GET request makes the server load and JSON-encode potentially millions of metric rows, exhausting memory and worker CPU on a SQLite-backed server (the common sqlite:///mlflow.db deployment). Fix: reject non-positive max_results and clamp it, e.g. `max_results = max(1, min(int(request.args.get("max_results", MAX_HISTORY_RESULTS)), MAX_HISTORY_RESULTS))`, and validate the parameter with the same schema used by the interval endpoint.

findings.title: Unauthenticated client can force full logged-models table scan via unbounded max_results
findings.description: Entry: /mlflow/logged-models/search (registered via handlers.get_endpoints(); handler _search_logged_models). Attacker: an unauthenticated network client of the tracking server, crossing from a tiny JSON request to an unbounded database read and response. Path: the schema only applies _assert_intlike to max_results (line 4235), with no upper bound, and line 4256 forwards `request_message.max_results or None` directly to store.search_logged_models. SqlAlchemyStore.search_logged_models (mlflow/store/tracking/sqlalchemy_store.py:3041-3081) performs `max_results = max_results or SEARCH_LOGGED_MODEL_MAX_RESULTS_DEFAULT` and then `models.offset(offset).limit(max_results + 1).all()` without ever calling _validate_max_results_param, so max_results=2147483647 (the int32 maximum) turns the query into a full table scan that loads every logged model and returns them all (`models[:max_results]` keeps everything). Nothing else on the path caps the value: auth is off by default, and unlike search_experiments/search_runs/search_datasets, this store method has no threshold check. Impact: a request of a few bytes forces the server to fetch, convert and protobuf-serialize the entire logged-models table into memory and into the HTTP response. Fix: validate max_results in the handler (e.g. _assert_less_than_or_equal(int(x), SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS_THRESHOLD)) and/or call self._validate_max_results_param(max_results) in search_logged_models before applying the limit.

findings.title: Unauthenticated DoS via unbounded max_results in trace metrics query
findings.description: Entry: /mlflow/traces/metrics (POST, handler _query_trace_metrics registered in handlers.get_endpoints()). Attacker: an unauthenticated network client, crossing from a small JSON request to an unbounded aggregation result. Path: the schema for max_results contains only _assert_intlike (line 3840), so any int32 value is accepted, and lines 3844-3848 pass it (or the 1000 default) to _get_tracking_store().query_trace_metrics. SqlAlchemyStore.query_trace_metrics (mlflow/store/tracking/sqlalchemy_store.py:3662-3710) forwards it to query_metrics, which executes `query.limit(max_results).all()` (mlflow/store/tracking/utils/sql_trace_metrics_utils.py:744) with no threshold validation. The caller also controls dimensions and time_interval_seconds, so the number of GROUP BY result rows can be driven up (e.g. one bucket per second per span name) while max_results=2147483647 removes any ceiling. Every returned row is converted to a MetricDataPoint, extended into the protobuf response and JSON-serialized in the handler. Nothing on the path (no auth by default, no store-side cap) stops it. Impact: one request can make the server materialize and serialize an arbitrarily large aggregation over the trace store, exhausting memory and CPU. Fix: enforce an upper bound on max_results in the schema (e.g. _assert_less_than_or_equal(int(x), MAX_RESULTS_QUERY_TRACE_METRICS) or the shared SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS_THRESHOLD) and call _validate_max_results_param in query_trace_metrics.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GET can load entire dataset records, exhausting server memory/CPU
findings.description: Entry: /mlflow/datasets/{dataset_id}/records (GET, handler _get_dataset_records_handler). Attacker: an unauthenticated network client, crossing from a one-line request to an unbounded database read. Path: the schema validates max_results with only _assert_intlike (line 5613), and line 5618 computes `max_results = request_message.max_results or 1000`; the value is passed to _get_tracking_store()._load_dataset_records(dataset_id, max_results=..., page_token=...). SqlAlchemyStore._load_dataset_records (mlflow/store/tracking/sqlalchemy_store.py:5210-5285) sets `effective_max_results = max_results or LOAD_DATASET_RECORDS_MAX_RESULTS` and runs `query.limit(effective_max_results + 1).all()` without calling _validate_max_results_param, so max_results=2147483647 returns every record of the dataset; the handler then builds a list of dicts for all records and json.dumps them into the response. Nothing on the path caps the value (no auth by default, no store-side threshold; the sibling search_datasets does call _validate_max_results_param at line 5076, this method does not). Impact: a tiny GET forces the server to load and serialize the entire record set of a dataset, which for evaluation datasets can be very large, exhausting memory and CPU. Fix: cap max_results in the handler (e.g. _assert_less_than_or_equal(int(x), LOAD_DATASET_RECORDS_MAX_RESULTS)) and/or call _validate_max_results_param in _load_dataset_records.

findings.title: Missing USE check on attach-model lets user hijack another's gateway credentials
findings.description:
Entry: mlflow/server/handlers.py:4889 (_attach_model_to_gateway_endpoint, POST /api/2.0/mlflow/gateway/endpoints/models/attach, whose before-request validator is validate_can_update_gateway_endpoint registered at mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:1487).
Attacker: an authenticated, non-admin user who has UPDATE permission on any gateway endpoint they control (e.g. one they created), crossing into another user's / another workspace's gateway model definition and the upstream provider secret it references, which they were never granted USE on.
The request body carries the client-chosen model definition id: AttachModelToGatewayEndpoint has the singular field model_config (mlflow/protos/service.proto:4799-4803), so the JSON is {"endpoint_id": "<endpoint I can edit>", "model_config": {"model_definition_id": "<victim's model definition>", ...}}. The validator validate_can_update_gateway_endpoint (mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:1218-1229) first checks only UPDATE on that endpoint, then does model_configs = body.get("model_configs", []) and returns _validate_can_use_model_definitions(model_configs); because the route sends "model_config" and not "model_configs", the list is always empty and _validate_can_use_model_definitions returns True on the empty list (mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py:1162-1163). Nothing else stops it: the handler at mlflow/server/handlers.py:4899-4905 parses GatewayEndpointModelConfig.from_proto(request_message.model_config) and calls store.attach_model_to_endpoint(endpoint_id=..., model_config=...) with no permission check of its own, and the store layer performs no authorization. The user then calls their own endpoint through the guarded gateway routes (mlflow/server/gateway_api.py:375 _create_provider_from_endpoint_name -> mlflow/store/tracking/gateway/config_resolver.py:145-241), which resolves the newly attached model definition's secret_id and decrypts the secret to call the upstream provider.
Impact: privilege escalation and cross-tenant credential use. The attacker's endpoint now runs on another user's/team's model definition, so every invocation is billed to and authorized by the victim's provider API key (or Azure api_base/deployment from the victim's auth_config), consuming their quota and allowing use of a private provider endpoint the attacker has no USE permission on, exactly the boundary the USE permission on gateway secrets/model definitions exists to enforce. It also lets the attacker silently repoint their endpoint's traffic through the victim's account and observe responses generated with the victim's credentials.
Fix: give AttachModelToGatewayEndpoint its own validator that reads the referenced model definition from the singular model_config (or the flat model_definition_id) and requires USE permission on it via _get_permission_from_store_or_default / _workspace_permission_for_gateway_model_definition, in addition to UPDATE on the endpoint; and make _validate_can_use_model_definitions fail closed (return False) when no model definition id can be extracted, instead of returning True for an empty or unrecognized list.

findings.title: Caller-controlled api_base in LiteLLM passthrough enables SSRF and key leak
findings.description:
Entry: mlflow/server/gateway_api.py:570-586 (POST /gateway/openai/v1/chat/completions; same pattern in openai_passthrough_embeddings 632-653, openai_passthrough_responses 678-719, anthropic_passthrough_messages 744-785, gemini routes 812-831/858-871), where the raw request body is read and passed as payload=body into provider.passthrough.
Attacker: any user who can call a gateway endpoint backed by the LiteLLM fallback provider (a user with USE permission, or any caller when auth is off), crossing the boundary that the server should only ever contact the operator-configured provider endpoint with the operator-configured credentials.
Path: gateway_api.py passes the unvalidated JSON body to LiteLLMProvider._passthrough (litellm.py:381-419), which calls _build_litellm_kwargs(payload) (litellm.py:85-91): kwargs = {**payload} first, then only the keys present in litellm_config.litellm_auth_config are overwritten. A typical secret supplies only api_key, so client-supplied routing kwargs such as api_base, base_url, custom_llm_provider, headers, aws_region_name or vertex_credentials are left intact and then splatted into litellm.acompletion(**kwargs) / litellm.aresponses(**kwargs) / litellm.anthropic.messages.acreate(**kwargs) (litellm.py:104, 167, 428, 456; the provider tests confirm api_base is forwarded verbatim to litellm).
Why nothing stops it: the passthrough handlers do not validate the body against a schema (unlike the unified invocations path, which uses chat.RequestPayload), and _build_litellm_kwargs has no allow-list or reserved-key stripping; only exact keys present in the stored auth config are overridden, so api_base in particular is caller-controlled.
Impact: the MLflow server issues an outbound HTTP request to an attacker-chosen URL while attaching the configured provider API key (it is part of the same kwargs), giving the caller SSRF into the server's network (e.g. cloud metadata or internal services) and exfiltration of the stored provider secret to a server the caller controls.
Fix: never merge raw client input into SDK kwargs. Build the litellm call from an explicit allow-list of request fields (messages/input/model/stream/temperature/...), and unconditionally overwrite or strip all connection/auth keys (api_base, base_url, custom_llm_provider, headers, api_key, aws_*/vertex_* credentials) from the client payload before calling litellm.

findings.title: MLflow caller's Authorization and Cookie headers leaked to upstream LLM provider
findings.description:
Entry: mlflow/server/gateway_api.py:578 (also 640, 686, 752, 818, 864), where each passthrough handler does headers = dict(request.headers) and passes the caller's headers into provider.passthrough(..., headers=headers).
Attacker: the upstream LLM provider (untrusted third party, or anyone who can observe traffic/logs there) obtains the MLflow caller's credentials; the boundary crossed is that MLflow Basic-auth credentials and session cookies must never leave the MLflow server.
Path: _get_headers (openai.py:342-366, mirrored in anthropic.py:398-433 and gemini.py) copies the client headers, drops only 'host' and 'content-length', and merges with result_headers = client_headers | result_headers. The provider's own auth headers are lowercase ('authorization', 'api-key'/'x-api-key'), while HTTP header names are case-insensitive but Python dict keys are not, so a client sending the conventional 'Authorization' (or 'X-Api-Key') key does not collide with the provider key; both entries survive and are handed to aiohttp's ClientSession (mlflow/gateway/providers/utils.py:14), which sends both values upstream.
Why nothing stops it: there is no allow-list of forwardable headers, and the intended precedence ('provider headers take precedence', per the code comment) only works for identical-case keys; Authorization is included in dict(request.headers) because the FastAPI auth middleware requires it on these routes.
Impact: every passthrough call leaks the caller's MLflow username/password (Base64 Basic header), cookies and any other caller headers to the external LLM provider, and lets the caller smuggle extra headers into the upstream request (the case-variant Authorization can also be used to override the provider credential at upstreams that read the first header value).
Fix: do not forward the client's headers wholesale. Forward only an explicit allow-list of provider-relevant headers (e.g. anthropic-beta) with normalized, lower-cased names, and always delete Authorization, Cookie, X-Api-Key, Proxy-* and hop-by-hop headers before the merge.

findings.title: Client-supplied api_base in gateway passthrough enables full SSRF
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/gateway_api.py:551 (openai_passthrough_chat; same pattern at lines 617, 659, 725, 793, 839). Attacker: any caller who can reach a gateway passthrough route, crossing from the public API into the server's internal network. The handler reads the raw JSON body with no schema validation (gateway_api.py:570-574, _get_request_body at line 63 only requires a 'model' key), pops 'model', and passes every other key as `payload=body` into provider.passthrough (gateway_api.py:584-586, 651-653, 692-694, 758-760, 869-871). LiteLLMProvider._passthrough (litellm.py:381-419) calls _build_litellm_kwargs (litellm.py:85-91), which is `kwargs = {**payload}` updated with the endpoint's auth_config, so a client-supplied `api_base` survives into the kwargs; the kwargs are then splatted into `await litellm.acompletion(**kwargs)` at line 500 (and the equivalent calls at lines 428, 443, 456, 465, 476, 487). LiteLLM treats `api_base` as the provider base URL, so the server issues its outbound POST to the attacker's URL with the endpoint's configured provider credentials attached. Nothing on the path validates the URL, resolves DNS against a deny-list, or blocks localhost/169.254.169.254/private ranges, and aiohttp/httpx defaults allow redirects, so an allowed host can also bounce the request inward. The endpoint must be LiteLLM-backed (any provider outside openai/anthropic/mistral/gemini, per gateway_api.py:222-233), which any caller can create in a default deployment and any authenticated user can create in a basic-auth deployment. Impact: full read SSRF from an arbitrary request body - cloud metadata theft (IAM credentials), internal service probing and data exfiltration, since the upstream JSON is returned verbatim to the caller. Fix: strip or reject request-body keys such as api_base/base_url before building LiteLLM kwargs, validate the effective base URL against an allow-list, and block internal/metadata address ranges after DNS resolution (with redirects disabled).

findings.title: SSRF via unvalidated gateway secret api_base to internal network and metadata
findings.description: Entry: mlflow/server/handlers.py:4507 (_create_gateway_secret, POST /api/2.0/gateway/secrets/create). Attacker: any caller who can create a gateway secret (unauthenticated in a default deployment; any authenticated user under basic auth, since CreateGatewaySecret has no BEFORE_REQUEST permission validator in mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py - only the after-create MANAGE grant at line 2157), crossing from the API into the server's internal network and its stored secrets. The secret handler accepts the caller's `auth_config` map unvalidated (handlers.py:4518-4524); mlflow/store/tracking/gateway/config_resolver.py:115 reads it back and _build_endpoint_config copies `auth_config['api_base']` straight into `openai_api_base` (gateway_api.py:186-192 for the azure branch and 203 for the azure provider). OpenAIProvider.base_url then returns that caller-chosen string (openai.py:295-302), and the invocation routes (gateway_api.py:412, 489, 548-886) reach `session.post(url, json=payload, ...)` in mlflow/gateway/providers/utils.py:14-18 with the provider's Authorization/api-key header attached. Nothing validates that api_base is an https provider URL, is on an allow-list, or resolves to a public address, and redirects are followed by default. The same unvalidated secret value is merged into `litellm_auth_config` (gateway_api.py:226-232, litellm.py:88-89), giving the identical SSRF through the LiteLLM provider for any non-native provider. Impact: the server can be steered to internal endpoints and to the cloud metadata service, and the stored provider API key is sent to the attacker-controlled host; the upstream response (including metadata contents) is returned through the invocation response. Fix: validate/allow-list `api_base` when the secret or model definition is created and again before each outbound call, reject non-http(s) schemes and internal, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses after DNS resolution, and disable redirect following on the provider HTTP clients.

findings.title: MLflow user credentials forwarded to upstream LLM provider
findings.description:
Entry: mlflow/server/gateway_api.py:752 (headers = dict(request.headers)) inside the POST /gateway/anthropic/v1/messages handler registered at line 722; the same pattern is at lines 578, 640, 686, 818 and 864 for the OpenAI and Gemini passthrough routes.
Attacker: the configured upstream LLM provider (or anyone who can read its request logs), crossing the boundary that the caller's MLflow credentials never leave the MLflow server.
Path: request.headers -> dict(request.headers) -> provider.passthrough(action=..., payload=body, headers=headers) -> AnthropicProvider._get_headers (mlflow/gateway/providers/anthropic.py:427-431), which only pops 'host' and 'content-length' and then does client_headers | result_headers. Anthropic's own header dict (anthropic.py:384-386) contains only x-api-key/anthropic-version, so the caller's Authorization header (the Basic credentials used to authenticate to MLflow) and Cookie are forwarded verbatim to api.anthropic.com. For the OpenAI passthrough (line 578) the provider's lowercase 'authorization' happens to collide and win, but the caller's Cookie and every other non-colliding sensitive header still reach api.openai.com, and Gemini (lines 818/864) likewise receives the caller's Authorization and Cookie.
Nothing on the path removes these headers: dict(request.headers) keeps them, BaseProvider.passthrough/BaseProvider._passthrough pass the dict through unchanged (mlflow/gateway/providers/base.py:156-166), and the merge logic only drops host/content-length. The gateway auth middleware never sanitizes headers either.
Impact: for every passthrough call, the user's MLflow Basic credentials (or browser session cookie) are disclosed to a third-party service, so a compromised or merely logging upstream provider can replay them against the MLflow server as that user, including admin users.
Fix: do not forward the client's raw headers; forward only an explicit allow-list of provider-relevant headers (e.g. anthropic-beta, openai-beta), and explicitly strip authorization, cookie, proxy-authorization, x-api-key and hop-by-hop headers in every provider _get_headers implementation, merging case-insensitively.

cases.checks: Of 1 published vulnerability in ollama/ollama@73257915, how many does a scan capped at $3 report?

detail.what: GHSA-F6MR-38G8-39RG (authz) Ollama 多个 API 端点缺少服务端认证导致未授权模型管理操作 (CVE-2025-63389) - routes.go

findings.title: Malicious registry can steal user's ollama.com token via auth challenge
findings.description:
Entry: server/routes.go:848 (/api/pull, same flow at /api/push server/routes.go:899) - the model name comes straight from the JSON body and may name any registry host ("attacker.example/ns/model").
Attacker: the operator of the registry the user pulls from (any unauthenticated third party the user can be induced to pull from), crossing from a third-party server to possession of the user's ollama.com credentials.
Path: PullHandler -> PullModel (server/images.go:587) -> makeRequestWithRetry (server/images.go:725) sends GET https://attacker.example/v2/ns/model/manifests/latest. The attacker answers 401 with an entirely attacker-controlled `www-authenticate: Bearer realm="https://ollama.com/token",service=...,scope=...` header. parseRegistryChallenge (server/images.go:853) copies realm/service/scope with no validation, and getAuthorizationToken (server/auth.go:53) signs the request with the user's private key (~/.ollama/id_ed25519, auth.Sign) and issues a GET to that attacker-chosen realm (server/auth.go:70), returning whatever token the realm responds with. makeRequestWithRetry stores it in regOpts.Token (server/images.go:746) and replays the original request to the attacker's registry with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (server/images.go:801-802).
Nothing on this path checks that the challenge realm belongs to the registry being contacted, that the requested scope matches the model being pulled, or that the issued token is only sent back to the host that issued it. By pointing realm at the real ollama.com token endpoint with scope `repository:<victim-namespace>/<model>:push`, the attacker makes the daemon authenticate as the user to ollama.com and then hands the resulting bearer token to attacker.example; the attacker can replay it at ollama.com to read, push or delete models in the victim's namespace. The same realm field can point at internal addresses (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/...), making the daemon send a signed GET there.
Fix: reject challenges whose realm is not on the same host as the registry being contacted (or a fixed allow-list), never forward an issued token to a host other than the one that issued it, and drop the challenge flow for arbitrary user-supplied registries.

findings.title: Blind SSRF: registry redirect target fetched without host or IP validation
findings.description:
Entry: server/routes.go:848 (/api/pull) - the model name selects the registry host, which the caller controls.
Attacker: anyone who can name a registry in a pull (or who can get a user to pull from their host), crossing from an external caller to the daemon's internal network and cloud metadata services.
Path: PullHandler -> PullModel (server/images.go:587) -> downloadBlob -> blobDownload.run (server/download.go:227). The code GETs the manifest from the user-supplied registry (server/download.go:254) with a CheckRedirect that stops at the first cross-host redirect, but then takes that redirect's Location anyway (`return resp.Location()`, server/download.go:266) and uses it as `directURL` for every chunk download (server/download.go:285). downloadChunk (server/download.go:329-337) then issues a plain GET with http.DefaultClient to that attacker-chosen URL.
Nothing validates the redirect target: no host or scheme allow-list and no loopback/private/link-local address block, and the Location header is fully controlled by the registry named in the request. The daemon can therefore be coerced into fetching http://169.254.169.254/..., http://127.0.0.1:<port>/... or other internal services, with the caller learning success/failure from the subsequent digest-verification error - a blind SSRF usable for metadata access attempts and internal port scanning.
Fix: only accept redirect targets on the registry's own host (or an explicit allow-list of known storage hosts) and reject loopback, private and link-local addresses before fetching.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SSRF via model name reaches internal network and metadata
findings.description:
Entry: server/routes.go:848 (POST /api/pull) - the model name is read from the JSON body at server/routes.go:860 and passed to PullModel at server/routes.go:886; the same sink is also reachable from POST /api/create via server/create.go:118 and server/model.go:31.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller of the daemon's HTTP API (any local process, and any network peer when OLLAMA_HOST binds a non-loopback address) crossing from API caller into the server's internal network.
Path: req.Model -> model.ParseName (types/model/name.go:135) -> IsValid only checks character set and length, and ':' is explicitly allowed in the host part (types/model/name.go:336-339), so a value like "169.254.169.254:80/ns/model:tag" passes -> getExistingName (server/routes.go:958) only case-canonicalizes existing parts -> DisplayShortest keeps the host -> PullModel -> ParseModelPath (server/modelpath.go:40-75) copies parts[0] into Registry -> BaseURL (server/modelpath.go:109-114) -> pullModelManifest builds the URL at server/images.go:694 and fetches it at server/images.go:698 -> makeRequestWithRetry/makeRequest (server/images.go:725-827). The request-body 'insecure' flag (server/routes.go:879-881) additionally rewrites the scheme to plain http at server/images.go:787-789, so internal HTTP-only services are reachable. Nothing on this path resolves the host or rejects loopback, private, link-local or ULA addresses, and there is no registry allow-list; the only host-related guard, allowedHostsMiddleware (server/routes.go:1423-1459), validates the incoming Host header for DNS-rebinding protection and never inspects outbound destinations.
Impact: the daemon is turned into a proxy for the caller. For any non-2xx status other than 404 the response body is read unbounded and returned verbatim in the pull error stream (server/images.go:756-762 -> server/routes.go:887), giving unauthenticated read access to internal HTTP services such as cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), localhost admin APIs and Docker sockets; the same primitive can scan internal networks.
Fix: validate the registry host before dialing - resolve it and reject loopback/private/link-local/ULA results (and re-check on every redirect hop, e.g. via a custom DialContext/CheckRedirect) - or restrict pulls to an operator-configured allow-list of registries, require https unless explicitly configured, and stop echoing upstream response bodies to clients.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /api/push can exfiltrate local models to any attacker-controlled host
findings.description:
Entry: server/routes.go:899 (POST /api/push) - the model name is parsed at server/routes.go:935 and passed to PushModel at server/routes.go:941.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller of the daemon's HTTP API crossing from API caller into the server's internal network and into the daemon's local model store.
Path: the caller-supplied name (arbitrary host with optional port) -> model.ParseName/IsValid (only charset checks, ':' allowed in host) -> getExistingName -> PushModel -> ParseModelPath (server/modelpath.go:40-75) -> BaseURL (server/modelpath.go:109-114) -> uploadBlob (server/upload.go:367-371, 391-392) issues HEAD/POST/PUT to the caller's host, and PushModel issues the manifest PUT at server/images.go:576 via makeRequestWithRetry/makeRequest (server/images.go:725-827), where the request-body 'insecure' flag again permits plain http (server/images.go:787-789). No allow-list or private-address check exists on any of these requests, and the inbound-only allowedHostsMiddleware does not apply.
Impact: the daemon uploads the named local model's manifest and blob contents to any host the caller chooses - data the API caller cannot otherwise read through the API (only HEAD /api/blobs/:digest and manifest metadata are exposed) - which is exfiltration of locally stored models from a shared or LAN-exposed instance; pointing the name at internal hosts also makes the daemon issue requests into its internal network, with upstream error bodies echoed back to the caller (server/upload.go:291-296, server/images.go:756-762).
Fix: apply the same destination validation as for pulls (allow-list of registries, or DNS-resolve and reject loopback/private/link-local/ULA addresses including on redirects), require https unless explicitly configured, and avoid returning upstream bodies.

findings.title: Ollama.com signing key token sent to any third-party registry host
findings.description:
Entry: server/routes.go:1503 (POST /api/pull, handled by PullHandler at server/routes.go:848; in client2 mode the request reaches Local.handlePull at server/internal/registry/server.go:340).
